title: Reading: matching features and short-answer questions
status: Owner approved v1.0.0 on 2026-10-18; teacher release to all eligible schools (optional extension lesson)
rights: Original Brains Heist LLC instructional draft, AI-assisted. Researchers, planners and findings in the passages are fictional and created for practice. Human editorial, key, mapping, difficulty and originality review pending.
prerequisites: Lesson 6 (reading for specific information) and Lesson 13 (TRUE/FALSE/NOT GIVEN and YES/NO/NOT GIVEN).
Teacher has checked actual Reading Screener and review states privately.
Optional extension: use when learners need practice matching statements to people and writing short answers within a word limit.

objectives.text: Match paraphrased statements with the people in a passage by locating names first and checking each idea against evidence.
Answer short questions with words from the passage, respecting the word limit and the question word.
Reject number and wording traps by reading the question word precisely.

levels.foundation: Researcher names circled with the teacher first; a five-word summary for each person before matching.
levels.core: Complete all thirteen questions in the time given, quoting evidence for matching answers.
levels.extension: Name the question word and expected answer type for every short-answer question.
levels.high_band: Explain why the most tempting wrong researcher is wrong for two statements.

blocks.title: Same name, different idea
blocks.mode: Opening challenge; learners decide before the reveal
blocks.instructions: Statement: 'Staff tried to block out distractions themselves.' Three learners matched it with Anna Kowal. Whose reason is best?

examples.label: Learner A
examples.text: The word 'distractions' is in her paragraph.
examples.comment: Weak: the word 'distractions' is not in the passage at all. Matching by repeated words is unreliable; statements are paraphrased.

examples.label: Learner B
examples.text: Her name is the first one in the passage, and the statements usually start at the beginning.
examples.comment: Wrong strategy: matching-features statements are NOT in passage order. Each one must be checked against the whole passage.

examples.label: Learner C
examples.text: 'Large numbers of them began wearing headphones' means the workers blocked the noise themselves.
examples.comment: Best: the idea matches ('blocked out distractions' = 'wearing headphones' because of noise), and the learner can quote the evidence.

blocks.title: Short answers: find, then copy
blocks.mode: Guided practice; answer alone, then check with a partner
blocks.instructions: Read the passage. Answer the questions. Choose NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS from the passage for each answer.

stimulus.title: What makes a good workplace?
paragraphs: Few questions have attracted more attention from employers in recent years than what makes people happy at work. Large companies now spend considerable sums on redesigning offices, offering new benefits and measuring staff satisfaction. Yet researchers who study the workplace often disagree about which changes really make a difference.

Dr Anna Kowal spent several years studying open-plan offices, which were introduced partly to encourage conversation between colleagues. She found that the opposite often happened. Because of the constant noise, many employees found it harder to concentrate, and large numbers of them began wearing headphones for most of the day, which reduced conversation even further. Professor Lewis Grant, meanwhile, followed employees at three companies for two years after they were allowed to choose their own working hours. Their reported satisfaction rose steadily, even though none of them received any increase in pay.

Other researchers have looked at the physical environment. Dr Sofia Mendes measured the mood of office workers before and after their workplaces were improved with better lighting and indoor plants. Both changes produced small but measurable improvements. However, Mendes points out that these effects were far smaller than those promised by the companies that sell such products, and she warns employers not to expect dramatic results.

For Dr Tariq Hussain, the most important factor lies outside the office altogether. His surveys suggest that a long journey to work reduces satisfaction more than almost anything that happens inside it. In his data, even a substantial rise in salary did not make up for an extra hour of commuting each day. Those who suffered most were parents of young children, who often felt that they were missing important time at home.

Professor Ruth Okafor's work focuses on something simpler: recognition. In a series of experiments, she compared the effect of a sincere thank-you from a manager with that of cash bonuses of a similar cost to the company. Surprisingly, the thank-you had a stronger and longer-lasting effect on motivation. Okafor believes that many organisations underestimate how much employees value being noticed.

What these studies share is a warning against assuming that expensive solutions are always the best. Before investing in new furniture or technology, managers might be wise to ask their employees what would make the greatest difference to them.

items.prompt: What type of office did Anna Kowal study?
items.evidence: Dr Anna Kowal spent several years studying open-plan offices
items.reason: The hyphenated word counts as one word; 'open-plan' alone is also accepted.

items.prompt: What did many employees wear to deal with the noise?
items.evidence: large numbers of them began wearing headphones
items.reason: The question word 'what' asks for a thing; copy it exactly.

items.prompt: How long did Lewis Grant's study last?
items.evidence: followed employees at three companies for two years
items.reason: 'Three companies' is a number trap; the question asks how long.

blocks.support: Foundation: the teacher circles every researcher name in the passage with the class before learners start.
blocks.extension: For each answer, write the question word (what, how long) and the type of answer it needs.

blocks.title: Matching features: researchers
blocks.mode: Independent practice under time (8 minutes); then check
blocks.instructions: Use the passage 'What makes a good workplace?'. Match each statement with the correct researcher, A-E. You may use any letter more than once. List of researchers: A Anna Kowal   B Lewis Grant   C Sofia Mendes   D Tariq Hussain   E Ruth Okafor.

items.prompt: A gesture that costs the company very little may motivate staff more than money.
items.evidence: the thank-you had a stronger and longer-lasting effect on motivation
items.reason: A thank-you is the low-cost gesture; bonuses are the money.

items.prompt: Workers tried to block out distractions themselves.
items.evidence: large numbers of them began wearing headphones for most of the day
items.reason: Headphones are a self-chosen way to block noise.

items.prompt: Sellers have exaggerated the benefits of a workplace improvement.
items.evidence: these effects were far smaller than those promised by the companies that sell such products

items.prompt: Freedom over the timing of work made staff more satisfied.
items.evidence: allowed to choose their own working hours. Their reported satisfaction rose steadily

items.prompt: Higher pay may not compensate for a long journey to work.
items.evidence: even a substantial rise in salary did not make up for an extra hour of commuting each day

items.prompt: Satisfaction improved although salaries stayed the same.
items.evidence: even though none of them received any increase in pay
items.reason: The same researcher can be the answer twice.

blocks.support: Foundation: learners first write each researcher's main finding in five words in the margin, then match.
blocks.high_band: For two statements, explain why a second researcher might seem possible and why they are wrong.

blocks.title: Short answers under time
blocks.mode: Independent practice under time (5 minutes); then check
blocks.instructions: Use the passage 'What makes a good workplace?'. Answer the questions. Choose NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS from the passage for each answer.

items.prompt: Apart from better lighting, what did Sofia Mendes study in offices?
items.evidence: improved with better lighting and indoor plants
items.reason: 'Apart from lighting' removes one of the two options.

items.prompt: According to Tariq Hussain, which workers suffered most from long commutes?
items.evidence: Those who suffered most were parents of young children
items.reason: Four words break the limit; 'parents' alone answers the question.

items.prompt: What did Ruth Okafor compare a thank-you with?
items.evidence: she compared the effect of a sincere thank-you from a manager with that of cash bonuses
items.reason: 'Compare ... with' points to the second thing.

items.prompt: What does the passage suggest managers should do before buying new furniture?
items.evidence: managers might be wise to ask their employees what would make the greatest difference

blocks.marking: Mark answers over the word limit as wrong even if the meaning is right (for example, 'parents of young children' in Q11 has four words). Record word-limit errors separately.
blocks.extension: Rewrite Q11 so that the four-word answer would be correct.

stages.title: Opening challenge: same name, different idea
stages.student: Decide whose reason is best before the reveal.
stages.teacher: Learners vote. Reveal the comments. Stress that statements are paraphrased and not in passage order.
stages.say: Match the idea, not the word, and always find the evidence.
stages.check: Learners can say why Learner B is wrong.

stages.title: Strategy: names first
stages.student: Note the steps: circle every name; write each person's main idea in a few words; then read the statements.
stages.teacher: Model circling the five researcher names in the passage and writing a five-word summary for Kowal.
stages.say: In matching features, the people are easy to find; the ideas are what you need to understand.
stages.check: Learners have circled all five names.

stages.title: Guided: short answers
stages.student: Read the passage and answer Questions 1-3.
stages.teacher: Allow 7 minutes, including reading time. Foundation learners use the circled names.
stages.say: Check the word limit before you write.

stages.title: Check short answers
stages.teacher: Reveal. For Q3, show how the number trap works.
stages.say: Read the question word carefully: how long is not how many.
stages.check: Learners can explain the Q3 trap.

stages.title: Matching features under time
stages.teacher: Time 8 minutes. No dictionaries. Remind learners that letters may be used more than once.
stages.say: One researcher can be the answer more than once.

stages.title: Check matching
stages.student: Check answers. For each mistake, copy the evidence sentence into your log.
stages.teacher: Reveal in pairs. Discuss Q4 and Q9 (paraphrase and repeated letters).
stages.say: If you cannot quote the evidence, you have not found the answer.
stages.check: Learners can quote the evidence for Q6.

stages.title: Short answers under time
stages.say: No more than three words: count them.

stages.title: Check short answers
stages.student: Check answers. Mark word-limit errors separately.
stages.teacher: Reveal. Use Q11 to show that a four-word answer is wrong even when the meaning is right.
stages.say: The word limit is part of the answer.

stages.title: My reading log
stages.student: Record each wrong answer as: wrong person, wrong idea, word limit, or spelling.
stages.teacher: Note the error types learners actually record. No band conversion.
stages.say: Your log tells you what to practise next.

stages.title: Exit ticket and homework
stages.student: Complete the exit ticket and take the homework.
stages.teacher: Collect exit tickets. Record the fresh-check date.
stages.say: Next time, circle the names first.

How I check a short answer before I write it:
My target for the next reading task:
homework: Find a short article that quotes three or more people. Write three statements that paraphrase their views, and ask a classmate to match them.
Practise counting words in your answers: write five short answers of no more than three words about the article.
Complete only the Brains Heist reading practice your teacher actually assigns. Suggested time: about 25 minutes.

blocks.title: Spending on cycling
blocks.instructions: Match each statement with the correct planner: A Marta Lindqvist, B Daniel Osei, C Helen Park. You may use any letter more than once.

stimulus.title: Spending on cycling
paragraphs: As more people take up cycling, city planners disagree about where money should be spent. Marta Lindqvist argues that nothing matters more than separating cyclists from traffic. In her experience, painted lines on the road do little to make new cyclists feel safe, whereas lanes protected by a kerb attract people who would never otherwise ride.

Daniel Osei believes that public bike-sharing schemes are the quickest way to change habits, because they allow people to try cycling without buying a bike. He admits, however, that many schemes have lost money.

Helen Park focuses on journeys that combine cycling with trains. She has found that commuters are far more willing to cycle to a station if they know there will be secure parking when they arrive, and she believes this is the cheapest improvement a city can make.

items.prompt: Some schemes have not been financially successful.
A low-cost change could persuade more people to cycle.
items.evidence: she believes this is the cheapest improvement a city can make

items.prompt: Painted markings are not enough to reassure beginners.
items.evidence: painted lines on the road do little to make new cyclists feel safe

items.prompt: People can try cycling before spending their own money.
items.evidence: they allow people to try cycling without buying a bike
items.reason: The same planner can be used twice.
